common_name: Shrub Live Oak (Sonoran Scrub Oak, Turbinella Oak)

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in rocky, well-drained soil; this slow-growing evergreen chaparral oak tolerates extreme heat and aridity once established.

directions: This Southwestern evergreen oak forms a dense, mounding shrub or small gnarled tree across Arizona, California, and New Mexico chaparral and sky-island foothills, usually staying under 20 feet without supplemental water. It regenerates readily from its root crown after fire or browsing, which makes it tough in naturalistic or restoration plantings but slow to size up as a landscape specimen. Give it full sun, rocky or decomposed-granite soil, and minimal irrigation once roots are established; overwatering in heavy soil encourages root disease.

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in any well-drained soil; this compact evergreen oak tolerates clay, lime, and coastal salt spray better than most small evergreen trees.

directions: Native to Japan and coastal China, this small evergreen oak stays compact and densely rounded, rarely exceeding 25 feet, making it one of the few true oaks suited to small-garden or hedge use. It is remarkably indifferent to soil pH and heavy clay and shrugs off sea spray, though it grows fastest with a warm, sheltered site. It has been used in bonsai and clipped hedging in Japan for centuries, a testament to its tolerance of hard pruning.

planting.note: Sow fresh acorns in fall or plant container stock in deep, moisture-retentive soil in full sun; this large, fast-growing oak needs room to reach its full spreading canopy.

directions: Despite its common name, this handsome deciduous oak is native to North Africa and the southern Iberian peninsula, not the Canary Islands, and is considered one of the most ornamentally striking oaks in cultivation for its vigorous growth and glossy foliage. Leaves often persist well into winter before falling, giving a long season of interest, and the species readily hybridizes with English oak where the two grow together. It grows quickly for an oak and needs a large site with deep, retentive soil to reach its full stature.

planting.note: Sow fresh acorns in fall or plant container stock in dry, calcareous, well-drained soil in full sun; this Balkan oak is prized for its drought resistance on poor limestone sites.

directions: This Balkan and western Anatolian species is semi-evergreen in mild winters, holding its leathery, finely toothed leaves well past the point most deciduous oaks have gone bare. It thrives on dry, calcareous slopes up to 4,500 feet elevation in its native range and is noted among collectors for shrugging off both drought and poor, rocky soil without complaint. Give it a warm, sunny site with sharp drainage; it has shown good hardiness without frost damage down to USDA zone 7.

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; this slow-growing shrubby oak stays compact enough for small gardens.

directions: Native to the mountains of northeastern Turkey, Armenia, and the Caucasus, this is one of the few true oaks that behaves as a large shrub rather than a forest tree, usually topping out near 20 feet even at maturity. Its bold, prominently veined leaves with showy yellow midribs give it an almost tropical look that is unusual among cold-hardy oaks, and it colors reliably yellow in autumn. It grows slowly and bears fertile acorns while still young, making it a good choice for collectors wanting an oak that fits a modest-sized garden.

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring where hot summers and sharp drainage are guaranteed; this semi-evergreen Mexican oak is not reliably cold-hardy outside warm zones.

directions: This semi-evergreen species from the cloud forests of eastern Mexico is grown for its long, glossy, avocado-like leaves and striking pinkish-purple spring flush, qualities that have made it a favorite among oak collectors in the warmer American South. It is a moderate grower reaching a modest 25 to 40 feet, appropriately scaled for residential sites rather than park-size plantings. Success depends on sharp drainage and reliably hot summers; it struggles in cold, wet winter soil.

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; water regularly through the first two summers, after which this Mexican oak is notably drought tolerant.

directions: Native to the Sierra Madre Oriental of northeastern Mexico, this red oak takes its name from its dark green, leathery, deeply wrinkled leaves that superficially resemble loquat foliage. It grows notably fast for an oak, is semi-evergreen in its northern range, and has proven surprisingly cold hardy for a subtropical species once established. Give young trees supplemental water for their first two summers; mature trees handle both heat and drought with ease.

planting.note: Sow fresh acorns in situ in fall where possible, since this deep-rooted oak resents transplanting once established; use fertile loam to heavy clay in full sun.

directions: This Middle Eastern deciduous oak from Lebanon, Turkey, and the Levant produces distinctively long, narrow, bristle-toothed leaves and fringed acorn cups unlike almost any other oak in cultivation. It tolerates heavy clay and alkaline soil far better than most oaks and performs best in regions with hot summers to ripen growth before winter. Because it builds a deep taproot early, it establishes best from direct-sown acorns or very young nursery stock rather than large transplants.

common_name: Canby Oak (Sierra Oak, Mexican Red Oak)

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in well-drained, alkaline soil in full sun; water during establishment, after which this fast-growing Mexican oak is quite drought tolerant.

directions: Native to the mountains of northeastern Mexico, this semi-evergreen red oak has become a popular landscape tree across central and south Texas for its fast growth rate and dense, glossy canopy. It tolerates alkaline caliche soils that stunt many other shade trees and holds its leaves through all but the coldest winters, dropping them only when temperatures fall into the single digits Fahrenheit. It needs little pruning or fertilizing once established and performs well as far north as the warmer parts of the lower Midwest.

planting.note: Plant grafted container stock in spring in any moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; this semi-evergreen hybrid tolerates urban pollution and coastal salt exposure.

directions: A naturally occurring cross between holm oak and English oak first raised in an English nursery in the 1780s, this hybrid combines a sturdy, classic oak framework with glossy, leathery, semi-evergreen leaves that give year-round structure. It tolerates urban air pollution, poor soil compaction, and coastal salt spray better than either parent species, making it a durable choice for street or seaside planting. Growth is slower and more compact than straight English oak, so it suits mid-sized gardens where a full-sized native oak would eventually overwhelm the space.

planting.note: Plant grafted container stock in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; this patented columnar cultivar is bred for narrow urban and street-tree sites.

directions: Bred as a cross between upright English oak and swamp white oak, this patented selection was chosen for its narrow, columnar form that fits sites far too tight for a typical spreading oak canopy. The glossy, dark green leaves have silvery undersides that flash in the wind and turn gold in fall, and the tree shows strong resistance to powdery mildew and borer damage compared with many street-tree oaks. Its hardiness and fastigiate habit have made it a standard choice for boulevard and parking-lot plantings across a wide range of climates.
